report:
**Conclusion: no—not on current evidence.** Whole-body vibration (WBV) should not be considered an effective, established way to prevent osteoporotic fractures.

The key problem is that evidence for the clinical outcome that matters—**actual fractures**—is sparse and imprecise. A systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials in adults ≥50 found that WBV *may* reduce falls, but the fracture evidence was too limited/uncertain to demonstrate a reliable reduction in fracture risk. Falls are relevant, but fewer falls do not by themselves prove fewer osteoporotic fractures.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6027066/

Some trials report small or site-specific changes in bone mineral density (BMD), but BMD is a surrogate outcome, not proof of fracture prevention. Studies also vary substantially in vibration type, frequency, amplitude, session schedule, participant health, and whether participants have established osteoporosis—making results difficult to generalize to osteoporosis sufferers.

For example, an 18‑month cluster-randomized trial enrolled 710 postmenopausal women and tested daily low-magnitude, high-frequency vibration; it evaluated falls, fractures, muscle performance and bone measures, but one trial of this type cannot establish WBV as standard fracture-prevention therapy, especially given low event counts and inconsistent findings across the literature.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24676848/

An earlier review specifically on WBV for fracture prevention likewise highlights that the proposed mechanism and preliminary findings were not sufficient to establish clinical fracture prevention.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3302025/

**Bottom line:** WBV might be a supervised adjunct for mobility/balance in selected people, but it should not replace proven osteoporosis fracture-prevention measures—risk assessment, strength/balance and weight-bearing exercise as appropriate, adequate calcium/vitamin D when indicated, fall prevention, and evidence-based osteoporosis medication.
